Done and pushed to #2635, 2026-10-14: 043508921b (DefStatics hands EvalInfo the keys it touched; the projection updates only those) and 9fb2bdf067 (unchanged spine roots kept): on Full Body the request 15.5–18.8 → 2.5–3.0 ms, statics after the edit 25–31 → 16–20 ms. closed_tickets.text: ^report(9) of the series: fresh ids and lack of reuse. Hazel mints ids two ways: Id.mk, a gensym (counter + random bytes), and names derived from a parent (Id.derive, Id.next, IdTagged.fresh_deterministic, v5 UUIDs), the distinction of Incremental Computation with Names (Hammer et al., OOPSLA 2015). Measure what Hazel can tell us today: (1) elaboration: analyzing the same program twice, which nodes come back renamed, and how many enclosing parts then fail the reuse check's hash (^report(8)'s 122); (2) experiment: name those nodes deterministically, and what reuse it recovers; (3) evaluation: ids minted per evaluation, and whether re-evaluated values ever share ids (why the call memo erases them). MEASURED 2026-10-13 (node, #2635 c4e64060f1; harness ~/.cache/hazel-diag/Test_Names.re, experiments issue009_experiments.patch, uncommitted): (1) the same term analyzed twice (Statics.mk_unmemoized; the memoized mk returns the same object): Full Body 667 of 111,462 nodes renamed, all minted by statics, 692 expressions then differ by hash; Witch 798/844, Scenes 210/237, Polygons 14/23. Sources: UserLivelit.mk_expand_dot_def (each use's dispatch on def.expand, FreshGrammar), StaticsBase.fresh_ascription, and 85 nodes from the Drawing library. (2) naming the first two by their use / what they ascribe (Id.derive by path): 667 -> 85 renamed, 692 -> 247 hash-differing. After a slider edit, incremental reuse: names held 943 -> 1,002, renamed 105 -> 46, reused 336 either way (the structural fallback recovers it): names change the check's cost, not what is reused. (3) evaluation mints 461,422 ids for the woods picture (33,847 nodes); evaluated twice, equal in structure, not by hash; the only shared ids are the program's own. (4) THE WORKER'S RESPONSE DIFF (ShareCodec, keyed by ValueHash with ids; instrumented build on 8342, ~/.cache/hazel-diag/sharecodec_stats.patch + share_moves.py): 8 woods figure moves, slots sent vs if structure-equal parts were references: worker->page 387,625 vs 347,920 (1.11x), page->worker 43,248 vs 21,728 (1.99x, small: ~5,400 a move vs 749,480 at load). The diff works because incremental reuse returns the same objects (~2,900 refs a move): identity survives through reuse, not names. (5) TIMED, 5 runs: after a slider edit, incremental vs scratch (node, medians): Full Body 502 vs 451 ms, Witch 857 vs 791, Scenes 1,547 vs 1,571; named about the same. closed_tickets.text: Merkle names at construction, then remeasure ^report(9)'s derived-names experiment. 009: content-derived names took the woods' evaluation from 1.9 s to 44.2 s. Today Util.ValueHash is a LAZY Merkle hash: a walk on first use, remembered per object in a WeakMap; TypHash (#2661) remembers types' hashes per object; nothing is hashed as it is built, and environments and closures only as generic values. Fix: compute each node's content name when it is built, from its children's names (already known), an environment frame's from its parent's and its binding, a closure's from its environment and body: a few operations per allocation, never a walk (the paper's constant cost). A content name is separate from the provenance id a step's result keeps for probes, or two values from one piece of syntax would share a name. Steps: (1) profile the derived mode first, to find where the 23x goes (walks, the WeakMap and GC, fallbacks); (2) the construction-time names; (3) remeasure gensyms, names kept and time; (4) then finish ^report(9)'s edits, including a CORRECTION: its claim that a hash that gives up is not remembered is wrong (ValueHash marks it unhashable, and a too-deep walk leaves objects marked busy for good). FOUND 2026-10-13: (a) the hashing is linear within an evaluation (each object walked once: 1,033,746 walked, 932,980 reused, the same every run); (b) but time per evaluation grew across a session (2.3 -> 5.5 -> 6.3 s; 44.2 s after a long run) with the same work and a growing heap: the side table (ValueHash's WeakMap). (c) Names kept ON each value (a hidden property, ~/.cache/hazel-diag/merkle_on_object.patch): flat, 2.2 / 2.5 / 2.2 s, about 1.4x fresh ids (1.6 s), names still kept (33,846 of 33,847). Full remeasure running.
closed_tickets.outcome: Matthew's hunch was right: the hashing was linear, but the side table it was kept in (ValueHash's WeakMap) made each evaluation slower than the last (2.3, 5.5, 6.3 s for the same work). Merkle names kept on the values (a hidden property, computed as a value is built) hold still (2.2, 2.5, 2.2 s) and cost 12 to 28% over fresh ids, not 23 times. ^report(9) updated: a section on it, two corrections, a theme-aware thumbnail. closed_tickets.text: Dress Up performance fix: dragging the friend where the cauldron's fumes turn (outside the witch's hut and inside it). The double-helix fumes make a drag slow enough to be a real UX problem. Likely why (from the code, not yet measured): every pointermove calls changed(), whose draw() replaces the whole picture (pic.innerHTML = svg); helixSvg draws each strand as short segments, about a hundred in all, each with four SMIL <animate>s on x1, x2, stroke-width and stroke-opacity, so every move re-parses them and restarts every animation, and the geometry they animate is repainted each frame. Matthew's idea: pause animations while dragging (pic.pauseAnimations() on pointerdown, unpauseAnimations() on letting go). Other ideas: draw at most once per animation frame however many pointermoves arrive; on a figure drag, move only the friend (its group's transform) and leave the scene's DOM alone, so the fumes neither restart nor re-parse; keep the scene in a group of its own that is replaced only when its settings change; make the fumes cheaper (fewer segments, or turn a group with a transform the compositor can animate). Measure first (performance before features): a drag's frame times in both scenes, before and after, against a scene without fumes. Changes go under Unreleased; no version bump or push until Matthew says.
closed_tickets.outcome: Measured, fixed, committed in kids-choice-games (3a27f9f), not deployed: it ships with the next Dress Up version, on Matthew's go-ahead. Measured in headless Chrome over the DevTools protocol (real mouse events, a 60-move drag of the friend, frames timed in the page). Before: the witch's woods took 8.1 s for the drag, frame gaps median 67 ms and p95 250 ms; inside the hut 4.2 s, p95 183 ms; the forest and the house took 2.0 s at 60 fps. The JavaScript was cheap everywhere (changed() about 2 ms); the cost was rendering. (1) draw() wiped the whole picture with innerHTML and put the cached scenery back, so the scene's 459 SMIL animations were torn out and re-registered on every move; now the scenery stays in place and the rest is replaced around it (woods 8.1 to 3.9 s). (2) The fumes cost even at rest, about 15 fps in the woods with no input; Matthew's idea, pausing the picture's animations while a drag is held, finishes it: both scenes now take 2.0 s at a steady 60 fps, like a scene without fumes. M's and D's room styles are still to come. Mind ^ticket(62)'s lesson: many SMIL animations (the fountain, the parrots) cost frames even at rest, so keep animations few, and check a drag in each room.
